answer: The plan is clear and well structured, with real traction. The main improvements are about substantiating claims, tightening the economics, and being honest about risks. 1) Strengthen the evidence. The 14% temperature-loss reduction and 8-12% bill drop are self-reported or point-level measures from a tiny sample (41 apartments, a single winter) with no control group and no weather normalization. State the sample size behind each figure, explain how bill savings were estimated, and acknowledge confounders. Also report conversion and retention: how many of 41 completed three fixes, how many reran scans, and what the 27 paying users said about willingness to pay at $59 versus the discounted price. 2) Fix the market sizing. The '$100M+' figure (3M households x $59 is about $177M) is a one-time hardware number that ignores that kits are reusable and the likely repeat-purchase rate is near zero. Show a bottom-up serviceable market built from reachable customers and realistic adoption, not '25% of 12 million.' Cite sources for the 44M renter, 12M target, and 2M landlord figures. 3) Make the unit economics and model coherent. Specify gross margin after payment, shipping, returns, support and app costs. Clarify the tension between a reusable $59 kit and one-time sales, and between landlord subscriptions at $6/unit/month and lending kits between units: how many kits does a landlord need, and what does each unit actually cost to serve? Give CAC assumptions and channels, since renters are hard to reach and landlords lack data and motivation, which is the very incentive problem you identify. Explain why landlords would pay at all (split incentive: tenants pay the bills). 4) Be explicit about the weakest assumptions. The utility data licensing line is speculative with no customer discovery; either validate with letters of interest or conversations with efficiency programs, or de-emphasize it. Revenue projections ($85K year one, $420K year two) need a line-item build (units, price, conversion) rather than a headline figure. 5) Address technical and regulatory risk. Explain how six cheap sensors over 48 hours reliably isolate air leakage versus conduction, how the model was validated against a ground truth such as a blower-door test or thermal imaging, and what accuracy you achieve. Cover FCC/UL certification cost and timeline, battery safety, and warranty/returns. 6) Sharpen competition and defensibility. The data moat claim is generic; explain the feedback loop concretely. Acknowledge direct low-cost threats such as smart-thermostat makers, utility-provided home energy kits and free audit programs, and DIY thermal cameras, and say why renters would choose Drafty. 7) Clarify the ask and plan. Provide a use-of-funds breakdown tied to milestones and a runway view, since $40K for 800 kits at about $24 is roughly $19K in COGS alone, leaving little for app, legal and marketing. Give a timeline with measurable goals (kits sold, paid landlord pilots, savings validated) and explain what happens if the funding is lower. State the entity and IP position (no entity yet raises questions on who owns the IP, especially with university grant funding) and plan accordingly. 8) Polish. Add a brief section on the team's gaps (manufacturing, sales, supply chain) and how advisors fill them, include a one-line traction summary up front, and replace qualitative claims ('fraction of an audit cost') with specific numbers and comparisons.
